newsitem.title: GERMANY: Krupp bid for Thyssen seen sparking restructuring.
newsitem.headline: Krupp bid for Thyssen seen sparking restructuring.

text.p: A hostile takeover bid by German steel and engineering group Krupp AG for rival Thyssen AG could spark a restructuring of Europe's steel industry, but its success is far from certain, analysts said on Tuesday.
A merger, if it went ahead, would create the third largest steel group in Europe in terms of output after British Steel and France's Usinor Sacilor SA.
With combined sales of more than 63 billion marks ($37.3 billion), a merged group would be better able to tackle overcapacity and force its rivals to restructure too.
But the layoffs that would inevitably be part of the process would not go down well in Germany's Ruhr Valley steel belt, where unemployment is already high.
Steel workers were up in arms even before Krupp confirmed its bid on Tuesday, while Thyssen declared it would seek partners to help its defence.
It was unclear where Krupp -- Fried. Krupp AG Hoesch-Krupp -- would get the funds for a bid or how the equities market would respond to a possible share issue, analysts said.
European competition authorities might also not look favourably on a merger, as the new group would account for nearly half of the German steel industry, they said.
Thyssen launched a pre-emptive strike on Monday by saying it expected a bid from Krupp that it was determined to fight. The company was due to hold a news conference at 1500 GMT.

"It's a wonderful idea, but impossible to see how they (Krupp) could finance it. Net of disposals, they would have to find about 10 billion marks. They would likely have to issue shares, and the market might not like that," said Terence Sinclair, steel analyst at Salomon Brothers in London.
"It looks to me like a classic case where the victim gets bid up, but the value of the buyer gets called into question."

Volker Firchau, analyst with the regional bank Bayerische Landesbank, told Germany's N-TV news channel that although Krupp had significantly reduced its debt since the 1991 takeover of Hoesch, it would probably not pay cash for Thyssen.

"Krupp-Hoesch has been very successful in restructuring but it still has problems in its ratio of capital to equity," Firchau said. "That's why I think it would be more likely to be a share swap than a cash payment."

Sinclair said synergies between the two companies in flat steel products and automotive pressings would make the merger attractive, but the inevitable job cuts and need for approval from competition authorities could pose obstacles.

Firchau said a merger of Germany's two main steelmakers could pave the way for the cost cuts needed to improve Germany's competitiveness against other European steel makers, particularly British Steel.
"In the steel industry Germany is operating with a cost structure that is not competitive," he said.
Thyssen said in January a tonne of crude steel cost it 160 marks to produce in Germany, compared with the equivalent of 155 marks in France and 120 marks in Britain.
Alan Coats of Merrill Lynch in London agreed a merger would create badly needed pressure on the European industry to rationalise.

"There is a need to focus on improving globalisation and improving profitability," Coats said. "The minimum unit for restructuring is about two million to three million tonnes, the output of one plant. It is hard to restructure on a smaller scale, and bigger players could more easily close one big plant."
Sinclair said the combined company could double its profit margin if it cut five percent of its 195,000 employees, but the final number would be more a political than a business question.

"The wild cards are the SPD (Social Democrats) -- which is powerful in Dortmund and won't like it -- and it would also have to be referred to the European Commission, where it might not even be allowed."
Coats said a merger could be a positive impetus for the industry in Europe.
"Steel companies have remained nationalistic, more so than chemical companies, and there could be more cross-border tie-ups," he said.

"I would hope that out of it comes a stronger steel industry. If Germany restructures, and the trend becomes more European, European steel makers will be more able to move into global thinking. Down the road, Asia will be a more powerful player, and there is a need to position for that."
-- Terence Gallagher, Bonn newsroom, 49-228-26097150 ($ = 1.690 German Marks)
